 Tata Motors PV revenue jumps 34 per cent to Rs 96,920 crore, but Q2 loss persists
 A Rs 6,738 crore restructuring charge offsets operating recovery as domestic sales hit a record and JLR faces pressure in China
 Published
 17 hours ago on
 November 13, 2026 
 By
 indiantelevision.com Team 
 Follow us on Google News 
 Follow us on WhatsApp 
 Share 
 Tweet 
 MUMBAI: Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited (TMPVL) delivered a sharp increase in revenue in the September quarter, but a hefty restructuring bill kept the newly demerged passenger vehicle business in the red.
 Consolidated revenue from operations rose 34 per cent year-on-year to Rs 96,920 crore in Q2 FY27, against Rs 72,349 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. Revenue was also up 1.2 per cent sequentially from Rs 95,799 crore in Q1 FY27.
 However, exceptional charges of Rs 6,738 crore, largely linked to employee separation and asset impairments, resulted in a consolidated net loss from continuing operations of Rs 5,451 crore. The loss attributable to shareholders stood at Rs 5,531 crore. In Q2 FY26, the company had reported a loss from continuing operations of Rs 6,368 crore.
 The operating performance showed a significant recovery from the year-ago quarter, when a cyber incident disrupted Jaguar Land Rover (JLR). Consolidated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) reached Rs 5,995 crore, against a loss of Rs 71 crore a year earlier. The EBITDA margin improved to 6.2 per cent from a negative 0.1 per cent.
 Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) swung to a profit of Rs 1,061 crore from a loss of Rs 4,897 crore. Profit before tax and exceptional items stood at Rs 403 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 5,462 crore in Q2 FY26.
 ” In Q2 FY27 TMPV continued to build on its strong momentum in the domestic business, while JLR delivered resilient volumes despite global market specific challenges and wind-down of previous Jaguar models,” said TMPVL chief financial officer Dhiman Gupta. “However, adverse mix and persistent commodity pressures weighed on margins.”
 Restructuring costs overshadow operating recovery 
 The Rs 6,738 crore exceptional charge included Rs 3,776 crore in employee separation costs, Rs 2,856 crore in asset impairments and Rs 161 crore for rationalisation programmes. A past service credit of Rs 55 crore partly offset the expenses.
 A net tax credit of Rs 884 crore, including deferred tax credits of Rs 1,745 crore, brought basic and diluted earnings per share to a negative Rs 15.02.
 For the first half of FY27, consolidated revenue increased 20.4 per cent year-on-year to Rs 1,92,719 crore. EBITDA rose 73.9 per cent to Rs 13,123 crore, with a margin of 6.8 per cent. Profit before tax and exceptional items improved to Rs 2,009 crore from a loss of Rs 1,512 crore in H1 FY26. The net loss from continuing operations for the half-year stood at Rs 4,592 crore.
 Marketing discipline meets rising incentives 
 The cost picture reveals different approaches across the domestic passenger vehicle business and JLR.
 Consolidated other expenses, which include advertising, sales promotion, freight, warranty and administrative costs, increased 11.2 per cent year-on-year to Rs 20,868 crore. However, they declined 8 per cent sequentially from Rs 22,682 crore in Q1.
 In India, lower fixed marketing expenses contributed Rs 206 crore to the sequential improvement in profit before tax between the first and second quarters. This helped offset higher employee costs and engineering and fixed overheads, resulting in total fixed-cost savings of Rs 156 crore. Standalone other expenses declined 1.3 per cent sequentially to Rs 1,232 crore, even as revenue rose 9.5 per cent.
 At JLR, the pressure came from variable marketing expenses, including discounts and customer financing incentives. These increased to 8.2 per cent of revenue in Q2 from 7.6 per cent in Q1, reducing sequential profit by £33 million. The company partly offset this through a £29 million reduction in fixed marketing and selling overheads.
 Consolidated material costs rose 35.6 per cent year-on-year to Rs 65,022 crore, accounting for 67.1 per cent of operating revenue. Product development and engineering expenses charged to the income statement declined 18.9 per cent to Rs 2,871 crore. A further Rs 8,582 crore of expenditure was capitalised.
 JLR recovers from last year’s disruption, but China remains a drag 
 JLR contributed Rs 75,420 crore, or 77.8 per cent, of TMPVL’s consolidated revenue. Its quarterly revenue increased 20.3 per cent year-on-year to £5,894 million, although it slipped 1.3 per cent sequentially.
 Wholesale volumes rose 24.7 per cent year-on-year to 82,500 units, led by Range Rover at 45,100 units and Defender at 30,000 units. Legacy Jaguar volumes fell to 800 units ahead of the brand’s all-electric relaunch. Retail sales declined 7.5 per cent year-on-year to 79,000 units.
 North America remained JLR’s largest market, with wholesale volumes rising 51.4 per cent to 27,100 units. The UK recorded a 70.7 per cent increase to 21,000 units. China, however, continued to weigh on performance, with wholesales falling 46.5 per cent to 6,100 units. The Chery Jaguar Land Rover joint venture reported a pre-tax loss of £38 million after local production ceased in June 2026.
 JLR’s adjusted EBIT improved to £67 million, translating into a 1.1 per cent margin, against a negative 8.6 per cent a year earlier. However, the margin was lower than the 2.8 per cent recorded in Q1 FY27. Profit before tax and exceptional items was £6 million, while £530 million in restructuring and asset write-down charges pushed the business to a post-tax loss of £451 million.
 JLR also reported a free cash outflow of £540 million, with investment spending in the first half reaching £1,766 million.
 “JLR delivered positive operating profits in the second quarter and first half of the financial year, despite ongoing global challenges,” said JLR chief executive officer PB Balaji. He pointed to the launch of three products: Range Rover Electric, Range Rover Sport Electric and the Jaguar Type 01, unveiled at a world premiere in New York.
 The company has lowered its FY27 guidance to an adjusted EBIT margin of 2 to 3 per cent on revenue of around £25 billion. It expects free cash outflow of approximately £1.25 billion. Its Enterprise Missions programme targets £1.7 billion in cost savings over two years, with the aim of reducing cash breakeven towards 300,000 units.
 India business posts record quarterly revenue 
 The domestic passenger vehicle business, including its electric mobility arm and joint operation FIAPL, delivered its highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs 20,423 crore, up 51 per cent from Rs 13,529 crore a year earlier.
 Wholesale volumes increased 39.5 per cent to 2,01,600 units. The business recorded a 14.3 per cent market share based on Vahan registrations, retaining the second position in the Indian passenger vehicle market.
 Electric vehicles accounted for 23 per cent of domestic volumes, while compressed natural gas models contributed 28 per cent. Petrol and diesel vehicles made up 37 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively.
 Monthly EV offtake rose 90 per cent year-on-year to 15,700 units. Tata’s domestic EV market share increased 380 basis points sequentially to 42.8 per cent, supported by the Punch.ev, Tiago.ev and the new Sierra.ev.
 The newly launched Aeris compact sedan added 4,000 units in its first month. Total monthly sales reached a record 75,400 vehicles in October 2026.
 Despite the volume growth, commodity costs squeezed margins. Domestic EBITDA stood at Rs 822 crore, with the margin declining 180 basis points year-on-year to 4 per cent. EBIT was a loss of Rs 63 crore, translating into a negative 0.3 per cent margin.
 Higher production-linked incentive accruals of Rs 516 crore, compared with Rs 313 crore in Q1 and Rs 125 crore a year earlier, along with Rs 128 crore in other income, helped bring profit before tax and exceptional items to Rs 26 crore.
 The domestic business generated positive free cash flow of Rs 825 crore in Q2 and Rs 1,945 crore in H1. It ended September with net cash of Rs 7,900 crore, comprising Rs 11,000 crore in cash against gross debt of Rs 3,100 crore.
 “We registered a year-on-year revenue growth of 51 per cent and our highest-ever quarterly revenues of Rs 20.4K crore in Q2 FY27,” said TMPVL managing director and chief executive officer Shailesh Chandra. “While steep commodity cost pressures remained a headwind, we responded through calibrated pricing and focused cost actions.”
 Net debt rises as investment and restructuring weigh 
 At the consolidated level, negative free cash flow of Rs 6,300 crore in Q2 and Rs 18,000 crore in H1 pushed net debt to Rs 50,800 crore at the end of September, up from Rs 42,200 crore in June.
 The September figure included Rs 53,000 crore of net debt at JLR and Rs 6,000 crore at TML Holdings. These were partly offset by Rs 7,900 crore in net cash at the Indian passenger vehicle business and Rs 300 crore at other subsidiaries.
 The consolidated debt-to-equity ratio rose to 0.76 times from 0.62 times in Q1, while net worth stood at Rs 1,05,126 crore.
 JLR ended the quarter with £1.84 billion in cash and total liquidity of £6 billion. The liquidity position was supported by a new £1 billion five-year syndicated term loan signed on 29 September and drawn in full during October.
 Management expects consolidated net debt to peak in FY27 before cash generation from new electric vehicle launches and cost-saving initiatives begins to reduce the burden.
